name: Denise Carter, step-down: DKA after cost-related insulin rationing

caseMeta.title: Step-down / telemetry: type 1 diabetes in DKA after months of cost-related insulin rationing, low potassium on the insulin infusion, a food-related low, and discharge with the medicines in hand (3 days, checkpoints at every 0700 and 1900)
learningObjectives: Manage an adult DKA protocol (2024 consensus) safely: isotonic fluids, fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h with no bolus, dextrose and 0.05 unit/kg/h once glucose is under 250, hourly glucose, and the resolution criteria (BHB under 0.6 plus venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher).

Apply the peripheral potassium rule: never more than 10 mEq per hour from all sources, hold insulin and replace when K is under 3.5 (K 3.2 at 0800), potassium piggybacks one at a time, magnesium on the other line, and restart insulin only when K is 3.5 or higher with provider confirmation; recognize why phosphate is monitored, not replaced.
Carry out the transition: basal insulin 2 hours before the infusion stops, carbohydrate-matched meal insulin, and prevent and treat the low glucose that follows a fixed meal dose with a small meal.

Identify cost-related insulin rationing and food insecurity respectfully (not "noncompliance"), and verify medicines, supplies, a food plan, follow-up, transport and teach-back with the actual products before discharge; do not credit referrals or coupons alone.

orders.name: Insert and maintain two peripheral IVs (left forearm 18 g, right forearm 20 g); no central line. Cardiac monitoring and strict measured intake and output; measure every void (no catheter)
orders.instructions: Remove the left 18 g IV at Day 2 0700 and keep the right as a saline lock; remove the last IV at discharge.

orders.name: ED resuscitation-level care with continuous rhythm monitoring and close neurologic assessment; reassess level of care after improvement
orders.instructions: Treat as severe biochemical DKA at first.

orders.name: sodium chloride 0.9% bolus (ED standing resuscitation order)
orders.instructions: Administer 1,000 mL over 1 hour IV Once, no added potassium.
orders.rationale: Hypovolemia with DKA (HR 124, BP 96/58, delayed capillary refill, dry mucosa). Adult protocol: 1-1.5 L isotonic fluid in the first hour (16.7 mL/kg at 60 kg).

orders.name: ondansetron (ZOFRAN) injection (ED dose, once)
orders.instructions: Administer 4 mg (2 mL) IV Once, slowly over 2 minutes.
orders.rationale: Repeated vomiting for 2 days. No ongoing PRN antiemetic order: reassess if nausea returns after the electrolyte changes.

orders.name: sodium chloride 0.9% 500 mL/h (ED, no added potassium)
orders.instructions: Administer 500 mL/h x 2 hours (1,000 mL) IV Continuous 0300-0500.
orders.rationale: After the first liter and K 5.3: continue resuscitation without potassium for the first two bags.

orders.name: sodium chloride 0.9% with potassium chloride 20 mEq/L, 1,000 mL bag
orders.instructions: 250 mL/h through a peripheral IV. 20 mEq/L is the most potassium allowed in a bag for this patient. PERIPHERAL POTASSIUM SAFETY PROTOCOL (two peripheral IVs, no central line; series rule): first confirm urine output of at least 30 mL/h and review the creatinine. TOTAL IV potassium from ALL sources across BOTH lines must NEVER exceed 10 mEq per hour. Never IV push; never use a 40 mEq/L bag (central-line strength). K 5.0 or higher = no potassium. K 3.5-4.9 = up to 20 mEq/L in the maintenance bag at the ordered rate (target K 4-5), or a discrete piggyback if one is ordered. K UNDER 3.5 = HOLD the insulin infusion, call the provider, STOP the potassium-containing maintenance bag (run plain saline), and give KCl 10 mEq in 100 mL premixed piggyback over 1 hour on a pump, one bag at a time, up to four in a row, by the current labs. Telemetry and IV-site assessment at least hourly during replacement; stop for infiltration or significant pain and re-site. Get an early K check during or just after the second dose and reassess before going past four. No automatic repeat series.
orders.rationale: K 4.0 (0445 specimen, reported 0500): replace by the peripheral protocol with 20 mEq/L. 250 mL/h x 20 mEq/L = 5 mEq/h, under the 10 mEq/h limit.

orders.name: insulin regular (HUMULIN R) 100 units in 0.9% sodium chloride 100 mL (1 unit/mL) infusion - DKA (fixed rate)
orders.instructions: Regular insulin 100 units in NS to 100 mL (1 unit/mL) on a dedicated peripheral pump and tubing, 6 units/h to start, NO bolus. Verify concentration and rate with two nurses at every bag and rate change. POC glucose hourly, including any hold. HOLD immediately if K is under 3.5 and restart only when K is 3.5 or higher AND the provider confirms. At the first glucose under 250: add dextrose-containing fluid and decrease to 3 units/h. Aim for glucose 150-200 while the ketones clear. Call the provider for: a glucose fall over 75 mg/dL in 1 hour (or a rise) while over 250 on uninterrupted insulin, glucose under 150, glucose under 50, recurrent vomiting, neurologic change, or worsening chemistry. Check the line, pump and volume status before any titration. If glucose is under 150 while ketones persist, call for D10-containing fluid and an insulin review (keep anti-ketogenic insulin running if K and glucose allow). If glucose is under 70: stop the infusion temporarily, treat the low, call for a restart plan.
orders.rationale: K 5.3 (over 3.5) so insulin may start after the first liter. 60 kg x 0.1 = 6 units/h; no bolus (2024 consensus). When glucose falls under 250 add dextrose and lower to 0.05 unit/kg/h = 3 units/h; keep the insulin running until the ketones clear.
nursingConsiderations: Hourly POC glucose; strict I&O; telemetry.
High-alert drug: two-nurse check of drug, concentration, rate and patient.
Stop only by order, after the first subcutaneous basal insulin dose has had its overlap.

medication.dose: 0.1 unit/kg/h = 6 units/h (6 mL/h); 0.05 unit/kg/h = 3 units/h (3 mL/h) once glucose is under 250
medication.importantInfo: Insulin stops ketone production; the acidosis (pH, bicarbonate, anion gap, beta-hydroxybutyrate) is the target, not the glucose. Insulin moves potassium into the cells: the blood potassium falls even though the body is low on potassium.

mar.adminDose: 0.1 unit/kg/h = 6 units/h (6 mL/h); 0.05 unit/kg/h = 3 units/h (3 mL/h) once glucose is under 250
mar.dispenseLocation: Central Pharmacy (IV room); premixed DKA insulin bag

orders.name: PERIPHERAL POTASSIUM SAFETY PROTOCOL: never more than 10 mEq/h from all sources; no 40 mEq/L bags; HOLD insulin if K is under 3.5
orders.instructions: PERIPHERAL POTASSIUM SAFETY PROTOCOL (two peripheral IVs, no central line; series rule): first confirm urine output of at least 30 mL/h and review the creatinine. TOTAL IV potassium from ALL sources across BOTH lines must NEVER exceed 10 mEq per hour. Never IV push; never use a 40 mEq/L bag (central-line strength). K 5.0 or higher = no potassium. K 3.5-4.9 = up to 20 mEq/L in the maintenance bag at the ordered rate (target K 4-5), or a discrete piggyback if one is ordered. K UNDER 3.5 = HOLD the insulin infusion, call the provider, STOP the potassium-containing maintenance bag (run plain saline), and give KCl 10 mEq in 100 mL premixed piggyback over 1 hour on a pump, one bag at a time, up to four in a row, by the current labs. Telemetry and IV-site assessment at least hourly during replacement; stop for infiltration or significant pain and re-site. Get an early K check during or just after the second dose and reassess before going past four. No automatic repeat series.
orders.rationale: Adult consensus: K 3.5-5.0 needs replacement; K under 3.5 = replace before and during insulin. Denise has peripheral IVs only, so this protocol caps the rate.

orders.name: Admit to step-down / telemetry: DKA in type 1 diabetes (cost-related insulin underdosing), prerenal AKI. Full code. Attending: D. Reed, MD (days) / T. Rivera, MD (nights)
Full Code

Continuous telemetry rhythm monitoring (recent electrolyte shifts) until discharge. Neurologic, respiratory and perfusion assessment every hour while on the insulin infusion, then every 4 hours and as needed. Vital signs per unit policy
orders.instructions: Call for new confusion, worsening abdominal pain, recurrent vomiting, palpitations or weakness, or ECG changes (peaked T = high K; flat T with U waves = low K).

orders.name: Strict measured intake and output every 4 hours with totals at 0700 and 1900; no Foley catheter; daily weight at 0700 from Day 2
Assisted bathroom activity; fall precautions (volume depletion, insulin infusion)
orders.instructions: Stand slowly; call for help to the bathroom.

orders.name: Ambulate independently as tolerated after nursing assessment, including hallway walks three times daily
NPO except ice chips and small water sips as tolerated (count all melted ice and water as PO on the I&O). No nutritional subcutaneous insulin while NPO
Point-of-care glucose immediately and every hour while IV insulin is ordered (including any hold), with an extra check at 1830 when the infusion stops
orders.instructions: Use the result for the insulin and dextrose steps (see the infusion order). Call for glucose under 150 on insulin, a fall over 75 mg/dL in 1 hour, or under 70.

orders.name: ECG 12-lead now (ED)
Initial labs (ED): chemistry, CBC, magnesium, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, arterial blood gas, lactate, lipase, pregnancy screen, urinalysis
Chemistry, magnesium, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous blood gas at 0445 and 0645 (expedited), then at least every 4 hours until DKA resolves
orders.instructions: Draw from an arm without an infusion running, or pause and waste per policy.
orders.rationale: DKA resolves when venous pH is 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate is 18 or higher, AND beta-hydroxybutyrate is under 0.6 (2024 consensus).

orders.name: HbA1c (add to the 0645 specimen)
Chemistry, magnesium, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous blood gas at 0745 (potassium has fallen to 3.6)

Consult endocrinology (review 1615), social work (0900 Day 2), case management (follow-up 1100 Day 3), pharmacy (access review 1730 Day 2), dietitian (1030 Day 2) and diabetes educator (initial 1430): each continues until discharge
orders.instructions: Cost-related insulin rationing, food insecurity and two part-time jobs without benefits are the reason for admission. Do not discharge with only applications or coupons and no insulin in hand.

orders.name: glucose 15 g rapid carbohydrate by mouth (juice 120 mL) - hypoglycemia protocol, nurse-driven
orders.frequency: As needed for glucose under 70 when alert and able to swallow; recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still under 70
orders.instructions: Rule of 15: 15 g fast carbohydrate, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still under 70. Once over 70, give 15 g longer-acting carbohydrate with protein if the next meal is more than 1 hour away. Hold meal and correction insulin during active hypoglycemia and call for a dose review. Basal insulin in type 1 diabetes must not be routinely omitted.
orders.rationale: Insulin therapy.

medication.freqKey: As needed for glucose under 70 when alert and able to swallow; recheck in 15 minutes and repeat if still under 70

orders.name: dextrose 10% injection (hypoglycemia protocol)
orders.frequency: As needed for glucose under 70 when unable to swallow safely and an IV is in place; recheck every 15 minutes and call the provider
orders.instructions: Give through a running peripheral line (never into insulin tubing). Repeat per response and call the provider.
orders.rationale: Insulin therapy; swallow not safe.

medication.freqKey: As needed for glucose under 70 when unable to swallow safely and an IV is in place; recheck every 15 minutes and call the provider

orders.name: glucagon injection (hypoglycemia protocol)
orders.frequency: As needed once for glucose under 70 when unable to swallow safely and no IV; call the emergency response
orders.instructions: Turn her on her side (vomiting is common after glucagon). Call a rapid response.
orders.rationale: Insulin therapy.

medication.freqKey: As needed once for glucose under 70 when unable to swallow safely and no IV; call the emergency response

orders.name: HOLD the insulin infusion NOW (potassium 3.2, under 3.5). STOP the potassium-containing saline and run plain NS (no potassium) at 250 mL/h. Start KCl 10 mEq piggybacks one at a time (no simultaneous potassium-containing fluid). Keep POC glucose every hour. Restart insulin only when K is 3.5 or higher and the provider confirms
orders.instructions: Telemetry; IV site assessment every hour during replacement. Draw the next chemistry at 0945 from a site away from the infusions. ECG now.
orders.rationale: Hypokalemia on insulin: replace before and during insulin (consensus).

orders.name: potassium chloride 10 mEq in 100 mL premixed piggyback
orders.frequency: Every 1 hour x4 sequential doses (0800, 0900, 1000, 1100), one bag at a time on a pump; 10 mEq/h maximum
orders.instructions: Peripheral IV, pump, ONE bag at a time: never more than 10 mEq per hour from all sources (no potassium-containing carrier fluid during the series). Never IV push. Draw chemistry at 0945 while the second bag finishes (from a site away from the infusions). Continue the third and fourth bags only after the 1000 result and provider review. Total 40 mEq in 400 mL.
orders.rationale: K 3.2 (0745) on an insulin infusion with a falling trend (5.3, 4.0, 3.6, 3.2).

medication.freqKey: Every 1 hour x4 sequential doses (0800, 0900, 1000, 1100), one bag at a time on a pump; 10 mEq/h maximum

orders.name: sodium chloride 0.9% (no potassium), 1,000 mL bag
orders.instructions: Replaces the saline with 20 mEq/L potassium. No simultaneous potassium-containing fluid while the KCl piggybacks run.
orders.rationale: Carrier fluid while the potassium piggybacks run: the 10 mEq/h limit leaves no room for potassium in the bag.

orders.name: magnesium sulfate 2 g in 100 mL 0.9% sodium chloride (premixed piggyback)
orders.frequency: Once, 0800-1000, through a separate compatible peripheral line
orders.instructions: Use the other IV (the potassium bag runs on its own pump). Recheck magnesium with the 1145 specimen.
orders.rationale: Magnesium 1.6 with falling potassium: low magnesium makes low potassium hard to correct.

medication.freqKey: Once, 0800-1000, through a separate compatible peripheral line

orders.name: Chemistry, magnesium, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous blood gas at 0945 (during the second KCl bag; released 1000) and at 1145 (released 1200)
orders.instructions: Phosphate is being monitored (replace only if under 1.0 or with cardiac or respiratory compromise or hemolysis); watch for new muscle weakness.

orders.name: ECG 12-lead now (potassium 3.2)

RESTART the insulin infusion at 6 units/h (0.1 unit/kg/h): potassium 3.6 (0945 specimen) is 3.5 or higher; provider confirmed. Finish the remaining two KCl piggybacks (potassium-free carrier saline until the fourth ends)
orders.instructions: Two-nurse check of the insulin concentration and rate. POC glucose every hour. Glucose is still over 250: no dextrose yet.

orders.name: sodium chloride 0.9% flush (peripheral IV)
orders.frequency: After the magnesium (1000), after the last potassium (1200), after stopping the infusions (1830), at 1900, and at 0700 and 1900 through the Day 3 1900 flush
orders.instructions: Disconnect the insulin tubing and clear the catheter dead space per policy BEFORE flushing a saline lock; never flush insulin-containing tubing into the patient. Day 1 1830 and 1900: 10 mL per IV (two IVs). After the left IV is removed (Day 2 0700) only the right IV is flushed. No flush at discharge.
orders.rationale: Keep the IVs patent; flushes count once on the I&O (infusion tubing priming is excluded).

medication.freqKey: After the magnesium (1000), after the last potassium (1200), after stopping the infusions (1830), at 1900, and at 0700 and 1900 through the Day 3 1900 flush

orders.name: dextrose 5% in 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium chloride 20 mEq/L, 1,000 mL bag
orders.instructions: Start at 200 mL/h as the first potassium-containing fluid after the fourth KCl piggyback has finished (never alongside a piggyback). Also DECREASE the insulin infusion to 3 units/h (3 mL/h) and keep it running: the ketones are not cleared. Two-nurse check of the new rate. Keep glucose 150-200. If glucose is under 150 with ketones, call for D10-containing fluid.
orders.rationale: First POC glucose under 250 (220 at 1200) after the last KCl piggyback: add dextrose and keep the insulin running (lowered to 3 units/h = 0.05 unit/kg/h) until the ketones clear. 20 mEq/L x 200 mL/h = 4 mEq/h.

medication.dose: 200 mL/h (4 mEq potassium and 10 g dextrose per hour)

mar.adminDose: 200 mL/h (4 mEq potassium and 10 g dextrose per hour)

orders.name: insulin glargine (LANTUS) SoloStar pen U-100
orders.instructions: Give at 1630 with the infusion still running; the infusion and the dextrose fluid stop at 1830 (two-hour overlap). Do NOT also give her former 2100 basal dose. Review rather than automatically withhold basal if she is NPO or low. Home continuation is 1630 daily.
orders.rationale: DKA resolved (1545 specimen). Basal insulin goes in 2 hours BEFORE the infusion stops. 18 units is below her prescribed 22 (recovery, recent intake): reassess for a sustainable basal-meal balance.

medication.importantInfo: Without a long-acting depot, stopping the infusion early means ketones return within hours.

orders.name: STOP the insulin infusion and the D5NS-with-potassium at 1830 (two hours after glargine). Start plain NS at 100 mL/h. Extra POC glucose at 1830. Disconnect the insulin tubing and clear the catheter dead space before flushing
orders.instructions: DKA resolved at the 1545 specimen (pH 7.37, bicarbonate 20, BHB 0.4, gap 10). Do not stop the infusion before the glargine has had its 2 hours.

orders.name: sodium chloride 0.9% (no potassium), 1,000 mL bag
orders.instructions: Start at 1830 when the infusions stop. Stop at 0700 Day 2 if she is tolerating oral intake and clinically rehydrated.
orders.rationale: Maintenance while she is just starting to eat.

orders.name: Consistent-carbohydrate meals, about 45 g carbohydrate each (an agreed 60 g lunch on Day 3 with carbohydrate-matched dosing); water and protein/carbohydrate snacks as needed. Document the carbohydrate actually eaten. No rigid restriction that prevents adequate nutrition
orders.instructions: Breakfast 0730, lunch 1200, dinner 1900.

orders.name: POC glucose before meals (0700, 1130, 1855) and at bedtime (2100); extra checks at 0200 on Days 2 and 3 and any time with symptoms
orders.instructions: Treat under 70 by the hypoglycemia protocol. Do not repeat a correction within 4 hours.

orders.name: Chemistry, magnesium, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous blood gas at 1545 (released 1600) to reassess the DKA
orders.instructions: Draw from a site away from the infusions.

orders.name: Chemistry, magnesium, phosphate, beta-hydroxybutyrate and venous blood gas at 1845 (released 1900): confirmation after the transition
orders.instructions: Repeat earlier or add testing if she gets worse.

orders.name: Chemistry, magnesium and phosphate at 0645 and 1845 on Days 2 and 3 and at 0645 on Day 4 while the electrolyte deficits recover; CBC once on Day 2 0645. Stop routine blood gases and ketones after the 1845 specimen (no further gases or ketones unless symptoms return). No standing blood draws after discharge
orders.instructions: Phosphate stays on the panels while she recovers (no replacement ordered; low phosphate improves with eating).

orders.name: ECG 12-lead at 1855: follow-up after the potassium and magnesium replacement
insulin lispro (HUMALOG) KwikPen U-100 - MEAL dose (fixed nutritional dose)
orders.frequency: With meals (Day 1 dinner, Day 2 breakfast and lunch), preferably within 15 minutes before eating
orders.instructions: Give when food is present; hold the fixed dose if the meal is unavailable or she says she cannot eat, and call for an alternative. Use the AC correction scale in addition.
orders.rationale: Starting meal dose with a consistent 45 g meal while basal catches up.

medication.freqKey: With meals (Day 1 dinner, Day 2 breakfast and lunch), preferably within 15 minutes before eating

Lispro 1 unit per 15 g carbohydrate eaten, immediately after eating, plus the written premeal correction scale. Glucagon 1 mg IM kit. Glucose tablets. Remove the saline lock; no extra flush or insulin dose at discharge.

stickyNotes.title: Potassium: peripheral IVs, 10 mEq/h limit
stickyNotes.body: Two peripheral IVs, no central line. TOTAL potassium from ALL sources on BOTH lines never more than 10 mEq per hour. No 40 mEq/L bags. K 3.5-4.9: up to 20 mEq/L in the maintenance bag. K under 3.5: HOLD insulin, call, stop the potassium bag, KCl 10 mEq/100 mL over 1 hour one at a time (up to 4), check K early. Peaked T = high K; flat T + U waves = low K.

stickyNotes.title: Insulin infusion rules (60 kg)
stickyNotes.body: 6 units/h (0.1 unit/kg/h), no bolus. Glucose under 250: add dextrose AND lower to 3 units/h (0.05). Aim 150-200 while the ketones clear. Call: glucose under 150, a fall over 75/h, vomiting, confusion. DKA is over only with BHB under 0.6 AND (pH 7.3 or higher OR bicarbonate 18 or higher).

notes.author: G. Alvarez, RN
notes.summary: Arrived with her sister after 2 days of vomiting and weakness; drowsy but arousable, deep breathing. Bedside glucose 690. Two peripheral IVs, first liter of saline running, cardiac monitor on. Reports reducing insulin because she lost her insurance.
notes.body:
**Arrival**
Denise Carter, 38, arrived at 0200 with her sister (Angela) after two days of vomiting and increasing weakness. Her sister noticed deep breathing and exhaustion this evening.

**Assessment**
Drowsy but responds to voice and answers orientation questions appropriately. Respirations are deep and regular, oral mucosa is dry, capillary refill is delayed, and the abdomen has mild diffuse tenderness without guarding.

**Actions so far**
Bedside glucose 690 mg/dL. Two peripheral IVs placed (left forearm 18 gauge, right forearm 20 gauge) and both are patent. Blood and urine specimens were sent and results are pending. The first liter of normal saline is infusing, cardiac monitoring is in place, and every void is being measured (no catheter).

**History she gave**
She has been stretching her insulin because she lost her insurance three months ago and could not afford refills. Her test strips ran out two weeks ago. She weighed 60.0 kg on arrival.

**Measurements**
Ventricular rate 122 bpm. PR 150 ms. QRS 86 ms. QTc 432 ms (Fridericia).

**Interpretation**
Sinus tachycardia. Mildly prominent, symmetric T waves with a narrow QRS. P waves present, PR and QRS normal: no sign of significant hyperkalemia. No ST or T-wave pattern of ischemia, no arrhythmia.

**Context**
DKA, potassium 5.3 at 0200 (resulted 0215). This mild elevation need not produce dramatic ECG changes. Insulin will move potassium into the cells and total body potassium is low: no potassium in the first two bags, recheck at 0445.

notes.title: ED Provider Note - DKA from Insulin Underdosing
notes.author: A. Shah, MD
notes.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis (glucose 684, bicarbonate 9, anion gap 27, BHB 7.2, arterial pH 7.23, K 5.3) with prerenal AKI (creatinine 1.5 vs baseline 0.7). Cause: cost-related insulin underdosing. Insulin 6 units/h after the first liter; no potassium yet.
notes.body:
**Chief complaint**
Vomiting for two days, weakness, deep breathing.

**HPI**
38-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age 18 (one remote DKA during influenza at 24). Three months ago she lost her job and employer insurance and began stretching her insulin: glargine about 10-12 units every other night instead of 22 units nightly, and lispro 0-3 units with some meals. During the last 48 hours she had thirst, polyuria, diffuse abdominal discomfort and repeated nonbloody vomiting; the last day she could not keep fluids down and took no insulin. Last glargine 10 units two nights ago at 2100. No fever, cough, urinary symptoms, chest pain or toxic ingestion. Her sister brought her in.

**Exam**
Drowsy but arousable, oriented when engaged. Deep regular respirations, dry mucous membranes, delayed capillary refill. Abdomen soft with mild diffuse tenderness, no guarding or rebound. No focal infection source on examination.

**Results (0200 specimen, available 0215)**
Glucose 684, Na 130 (corrected about 139), **K 5.3**, Cl 94, **bicarbonate 9, anion gap 27**, BUN 32, **creatinine 1.5** (baseline 0.7), **BHB 7.2**, phosphate 4.8, Mg 1.9. Arterial blood gas pH 7.23, pCO2 22 (expected 21.5 +/- 2: appropriate compensation). WBC 15.2, Hgb 15.7, platelets 326, lactate 1.7, lipase 30, pregnancy screen negative.

**Assessment / plan**
1. **DKA** with severe biochemical features (bicarbonate 9, BHB 7.2) although the pH is 7.23: remain in the resuscitation area with ICU-level nursing during initial treatment.
2. Volume depletion with **prerenal AKI**: normal saline 1 L over 1 hour, then 500 mL/h.
3. **Insulin**: regular insulin 6 units/h (0.1 unit/kg/h at 60 kg), no bolus, to start after the first liter and with K 5.3 confirmed. No potassium in the first two bags; recheck chemistry at 0445.
4. Ondansetron 4 mg IV once for vomiting.
5. **Precipitant**: cost-related insulin underdosing; no focal infection on history or examination (urinalysis pending). Reassess the white count rather than treat it as sepsis.
6. Peripheral IV potassium safety protocol written (never more than 10 mEq/h).

The first liter of saline finished at 0300 and normal saline is now running at 500 mL/h. Regular insulin 6 units/h (1 unit/mL) was started at 0300, with no bolus, after independent pump and concentration verification with a second nurse.

The next glucose check is due at 0400; the latest bedside value is the 0300 result of 650 mg/dL.

Denise is more alert and reports less nausea after the single ondansetron dose (0225). Both peripheral sites are soft and patent. Urine is being collected and measured without a catheter. The 0330 vital-sign set has been entered in the ED flowsheet.

notes.author: A. Shah, MD

notes.body:
The 0445 specimen showed improving acidosis with bicarbonate 12, BHB 5.0, potassium 4.0 and creatinine 1.2. Saline containing 20 mEq per liter of potassium was started at 0500 at 250 mL per hour (5 mEq/h).

She is now alert, protects her airway and reports improving abdominal discomfort without focal tenderness. Glucose has fallen at about 60 mg/dL per hour since the infusion began.

Her course is compatible with improving moderate DKA, and transfer to an appropriately staffed step-down unit is reasonable after another assessment and the 0645 labs. The unit has an approved IV-insulin pathway and hourly glucose capability. She is not ready for subcutaneous transition: hourly bedside glucose and scheduled electrolyte checks must continue.

notes.title: ED to Step-Down Handoff (SBAR)
notes.author: G. Alvarez, RN
notes.summary: Handoff to step-down: DKA improving on insulin 6 units/h (since 0300) and saline with potassium 20 mEq/L at 250 mL/h (since 0500). Two patent IVs, voiding. 0645 labs pending. Sister has her daughter and may join teaching.
notes.body:
**Situation**
Denise Carter, 38, is going to step-down/telemetry for diabetic ketoacidosis from cost-related insulin underdosing. Bedside handoff, pump verification and a second-nurse check of the insulin concentration and rate are planned at the bedside on arrival.

**Background**
Type 1 diabetes since age 18; two days of vomiting; no insulin the day before arrival. Allergies: none known. Full code. Weight 60.0 kg (dosing weight). ED treatment: normal saline 1,000 mL (0200-0300), ondansetron 4 mg IV once (0225), normal saline 500 mL/h (0300-0500), regular insulin 6 units/h from 0300, and normal saline with potassium chloride 20 mEq/L at 250 mL/h from 0500 (5 mEq/h).

**Assessment**
Alert, conversant, abdominal discomfort improving, still breathing deeply. Glucose 470 at 0600 (falling about 60 per hour). Two patent peripheral IVs (left forearm 18 g, right forearm 20 g); no central line. About 500 mL of urine measured since 0200 and about 250 mL of emesis (0215). The 0645 specimen has been drawn and results are pending.

**Recommendation**
Hourly glucose, keep the rhythm on the monitor, and check the potassium result when it releases: the potassium has been falling with insulin. Her sister Angela has her 12-year-old daughter and Denise agrees to involving her sister in teaching. Pace teaching around fatigue and nausea.

notes.title: Step-Down Admission History and Physical
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: Admitted to step-down: DKA improving but not resolved (0645: glucose 424, bicarbonate 13, gap 19, BHB 4.1, K 3.6, Mg 1.6, creatinine 1.0). Continue insulin 6 units/h and saline with potassium 20 mEq/L; early repeat panel for the falling potassium. Cost is the precipitant.
notes.body:
**Reason for admission**
Diabetic ketoacidosis from cost-related insulin underdosing, with prerenal acute kidney injury.

**HPI**
38-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes since age 18. Three months ago she lost her full-time job and insurance; she now works variable shifts at two part-time jobs without benefits. Insulin refills competed with rent and groceries, so she stretched glargine to about 10-12 units every other night and took lispro 0-3 units with some meals. Two days of vomiting, thirst and polyuria ended with no insulin the day before arrival. ED course: 2.5 L saline, ondansetron once, insulin 6 units/h from 0300, potassium-containing saline from 0500.

**Past history**
Type 1 diabetes at 18; one DKA at 24 during influenza. No CKD, heart failure, coronary disease, neuropathy or gastroparesis; baseline creatinine 0.7. No SGLT2 inhibitor. One uncomplicated childbirth.

**Medications**
Prescribed: glargine U-100 (LANTUS) 22 units nightly at 2100; lispro U-100 (HUMALOG) 6 units with each full meal plus 1 unit per 50 mg/dL above 200 before meals; no pump. Actually taking: glargine 10-12 units every other night, lispro 0-3 units. **Allergies:** none known.

**Social / family**
Lives with her 12-year-old daughter in rented housing; household gross income about $2,600 a month. Skips meals so her daughter can eat. Working phone with intermittent data; no reliable car. Meter works but strips ran out two weeks ago. No tobacco, drugs or heavy alcohol. Sister Angela has the daughter. Mother has autoimmune hypothyroidism; father has type 2 diabetes and hypertension.

**Exam**
Alert, tired, dry mouth, deep respirations, mild diffuse abdominal soreness without guarding. Two peripheral IVs; no central line. Telemetry: sinus tachycardia, no ectopy.

**Data**
0645 specimen (just released): glucose 424, bicarbonate 13, anion gap 19, BHB 4.1, potassium 3.6, magnesium 1.6, creatinine 1.0. Phosphate has fallen from 4.8 to 2.0 with treatment.

**Assessment / plan**
1. **DKA, improving but not resolved.** Continue regular insulin 6 units/h and the current saline with potassium 20 mEq/L at 250 mL/h (5 mEq/h; no higher potassium concentration through peripheral IVs). Hourly glucose.
2. **Potassium is falling toward the insulin-hold threshold** (5.3, 4.0, 3.6): obtain an early repeat panel at 0745 (Mg and phosphate included). Insulin is held if K is under 3.5.
3. **Phosphate** 2.0: monitor with each panel and watch for weakness; replace only if under 1.0 or with heart or breathing problems or hemolysis.
4. **Prerenal AKI** (creatinine 1.5 to 1.0): strict measured I&O, no catheter.
5. **Cost-related insulin rationing and food insecurity:** consult endocrinology, social work, case management, pharmacy, dietitian and diabetes education. Discharge planning must secure actual supplies and follow-up, not only prescriptions.
6. Fall precautions; assisted bathroom activity; telemetry.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Note - Critical Potassium
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: Critical K 3.2 (0745 specimen, called at 0800) with Mg 1.6, phosphate 1.8, pH 7.30, BHB 3.5. Insulin held per protocol; plain saline; KCl 10 mEq piggybacks one at a time x4; magnesium 2 g on the other IV; ECG now. Vomited 150 mL at 0730.
notes.body:
The laboratory called potassium 3.2 at 0800 from the 0745 specimen. The trend on insulin is 5.3, 4.0, 3.6, 3.2. Same specimen: glucose 360, bicarbonate 14, anion gap 17, BHB 3.5, venous pH 7.30, magnesium 1.6, phosphate 1.8.

Per the peripheral potassium protocol: the insulin infusion is held (K under 3.5); the saline carrying potassium is replaced by plain saline at 250 mL/h; KCl 10 mEq in 100 mL piggybacks run one at a time, four in a row, with no simultaneous potassium-containing fluid (10 mEq/h maximum); magnesium sulfate 2 g runs over 2 hours on the other IV. A 12-lead ECG is ordered now, with telemetry and hourly site checks.

She vomited about 150 mL at 0730 after sips of water and now has no palpitations or new muscle weakness. A pH of 7.30 with BHB 3.5 is not resolved DKA. The next chemistry will be drawn at 0945 during the second potassium bag, from a site away from the infusions; insulin restarts only when K is 3.5 or higher and I confirm.

notes.author: R. Okonkwo, MD
notes.summary: Sinus rhythm 96, PR 158 ms, QRS 86 ms, QTc 460 ms (Fridericia). Flattened T waves with small distinct U waves, no ectopy (potassium 3.2, magnesium 1.6 at 0745).
notes.body:
**Measurements**
Ventricular rate 96 bpm. PR 158 ms. QRS 86 ms. QTc 460 ms (Fridericia; the U wave is identified separately and not included in the QT).

**Interpretation**
Sinus rhythm. Flattened T waves with small, distinct U waves best seen in V2-V3. No ventricular ectopy. Compared with 0205: rate slower (122 to 96), the prominent T waves are gone and a low-potassium pattern has appeared.

**Context**
Potassium 5.3 (0200), 4.0 (0445), 3.6 (0645), 3.2 (0745, reported 0800) and magnesium 1.6 on the insulin infusion. Correct both deficits and keep her on telemetry. Never infer a normal potassium from the ECG alone.

notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: 0945 specimen: K 3.6, creatinine 0.9, BHB 3.0 (DKA not resolved). Insulin restarted 6 units/h at 1000; last two KCl bags approved. Phosphate 1.6 is being monitored, not replaced.
notes.body:
**Subjective**
Tired, no vomiting since 0730, denies palpitations and weakness.

**Objective**
The 0945 specimen (drawn during the second replacement bag) released at 1000: potassium 3.6, creatinine 0.9, bicarbonate 14, gap 16, BHB 3.0, venous pH 7.31, magnesium 1.6, phosphate 1.6. Urine output has been adequate. Glucose 330 at 1000.

**Assessment / plan**
1. **Hypokalemia, improving:** potassium is 3.5 or higher, so I approve **insulin restart at 6 units/h at 1000** and completion of the remaining two KCl 10 mEq bags. Keep the carrier saline free of potassium until the fourth piggyback ends. Next chemistry at 1145.
2. **Magnesium:** replacement is complete; recheck on the 1145 specimen.
3. **Phosphate 1.6, falling slowly with treatment:** no weakness and no heart or breathing problem, so it is monitored, not replaced (replace if under 1.0 or with compromise or hemolysis). It will be rechecked with each panel.
4. **DKA not resolved:** glucose is still above the dextrose threshold and BHB remains 3.0. Keep hourly glucose.

notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: Four KCl bags finished (40 mEq). 1145: K 4.0, bicarbonate 16, BHB 1.6, Mg 1.9, phosphate 1.5. Glucose 220 at 1200: D5NS with KCl 20 mEq/L at 200 mL/h and insulin down to 3 units/h; ketones not cleared. Phosphate monitored, not replaced.
notes.body:
The four potassium piggybacks have finished (40 mEq in 400 mL, completed at 1200). The 1145 specimen released at 1200: potassium 4.0, bicarbonate 16, anion gap 13, BHB 1.6, venous pH 7.33, creatinine 0.8, magnesium 1.9 (replaced), phosphate 1.5.

Bedside glucose at 1200 was 220, below 250, so dextrose-containing fluid is added: D5NS with potassium 20 mEq/L at 200 mL/h (4 mEq/h of potassium) and the regular insulin is reduced to 3 units/h (0.05 unit/kg/h). Insulin must continue: the bicarbonate is 16 and the BHB is 1.6, so DKA is not resolved even though the glucose has improved.

Phosphate 1.5 is low from treatment and recovery. She has no weakness and no heart or breathing compromise, so no phosphate is ordered; it is monitored on each panel and should improve with eating. No vomiting since 0730; she is taking small sips. Peripheral sites intact. Next panel at 1545.

notes.title: Diabetes Education - Initial Assessment
notes.author: O. Hart, RN, CDCES
notes.summary: Describes stretching basal insulin and skipping meal insulin to make supplies last; thought she did not need insulin when she could not eat. No blame; basal vs meal insulin explained. Pen teaching waits until the regimen is settled.
notes.body:
Denise describes stretching basal insulin and skipping meal insulin to make supplies last. She says she believed insulin was unnecessary when vomiting prevented eating.

We discussed the separate roles of basal and meal insulin without assigning blame for the cost barrier. She can explain that withholding all insulin can allow ketones to build even when she is not eating.

She is still receiving IV insulin, so full pen demonstrations will wait until she is rested and the discharge regimen is settled. I asked pharmacy and case management to make meter strips, needles, food access and insulin affordability part of the same plan.

notes.title: Endocrinology Consult - DKA Resolved, Transition Plan
notes.author: V. Lee, MD
notes.summary: 1545 specimen: glucose 184, BHB 0.4, venous pH 7.37, bicarbonate 20, gap 10: DKA resolved by the 2024 definition. Glargine 18 units at 1630, insulin infusion until 1830 (2-hour overlap), lispro 4 units with a 45 g meal plus correction.
notes.body:
The 1545 results released at 1600: glucose 184, BHB 0.4, venous pH 7.37, bicarbonate 20, anion gap 10. DKA now meets the 2024 consensus resolution definition (BHB under 0.6 plus venous pH 7.3 or higher or bicarbonate 18 or higher). Neither the 1145 bicarbonate of 16 nor a nearly closed gap would have allowed an earlier transition with a BHB of 1.6.

She is alert and ready to try a consistent-carbohydrate meal. **Give glargine 18 units at 1630 and continue the IV insulin until 1830** for a full two-hour overlap; stop the dextrose fluid at the same time. Do not also give the former 2100 basal dose.

Begin lispro 4 units with a full 45 g meal plus the conservative premeal correction order (no bedtime correction), with attention to actual food available and appetite. The lower regimen compared with her former prescription (glargine 22 units, lispro 6 units) reflects recovery, recent intake and the need to reassess a sustainable basal-meal balance.

notes.author: D. Reed, MD

notes.body:
Glargine 18 units was given at 1630 and independently verified. The insulin infusion continued for two hours and was stopped at 1830 with bedside glucose 188. The dextrose-containing fluid was stopped at the same time and plain saline is running at 100 mL/h.

Denise is alert, reports that nausea has resolved and is waiting for dinner. The confirmatory 1845 specimen has not yet been collected and no result from it is available. The evening team will give the prescribed meal dose when food is present and will not give a duplicate bedtime glargine dose.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Night Note - Evening Assessment
notes.author: T. Rivera, MD
notes.summary: 1845 results: K 3.9, bicarbonate 22, gap 9, BHB 0.3 (stable off IV insulin); ECG normal. Dinner: lispro 4 units, ate the full 45 g. Her glargine is now once a day at 1630: no 2100 dose tonight.
notes.body:
The 1845 results are available: potassium 3.9, bicarbonate 22, anion gap 9, BHB 0.3. The 1855 ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with normal T waves and no U waves. Glucose before dinner was 190.

Denise received the dinner lispro dose (4 units) after food arrived and ate the full 45 g meal. She is comfortable without recurrent vomiting or abdominal pain.

She tells me she had been choosing groceries for her daughter over refilling her own insulin. Her sister has confirmed childcare for tonight, and Denise consents to keeping her informed. Plan: bedtime glucose at 2100 with no correction, an extra check at 0200, and no 2100 basal dose; her next glargine is tomorrow at 1630.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Progress Note - Day 2 Morning
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: DKA and AKI resolved: bicarbonate 24, gap 9, K 3.7, creatinine 0.7; glucose 148 before breakfast. Stop IV fluids, remove one IV, walk. Phosphate 2.3 still a little low: keep checking. Not ready for discharge: medicine access, food and independent dosing unresolved.
notes.body:
**Subjective**
No nausea or vomiting, abdominal soreness gone, appetite variable. Says she often skips lunch.

**Objective**
The 0645 panel released at 0700: potassium 3.7, bicarbonate 24, anion gap 9, creatinine back to 0.7, magnesium 1.8, phosphate 2.3, WBC 9.0 (the admission white count was stress-related; no infection found). The overnight safety glucose was 156 and the prebreakfast value is 148. HbA1c from Day 1 is 11.8%, an average glucose near 290 over the past three months, consistent with the insulin rationing.

**Assessment / plan**
1. **DKA and prerenal AKI resolved** without recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms. She is eating and drinking, so IV fluids stop now, the left peripheral IV comes out (the right stays as a saline lock), and she walks with assessment.
2. **Phosphate** is improving but still slightly low (2.3): continue the planned chemistry surveillance.
3. **Insulin:** glargine 18 units at 1630; lispro 4 units with a full 45 g meal plus correction.
4. **Discharge is not appropriate yet:** medicine access, food security and independent use of the final regimen remain unresolved. Social work, dietitian and pharmacy are seeing her today.

notes.title: Social Work Assessment - Insulin Access and Food Security
notes.author: L. Brooks, LCSW
notes.summary: Lost insurance 3 months ago; two part-time jobs; skips meals so her daughter can eat. Benefits screening started with consent. No coverage approval yet. Plan: leave with an insulin and supply bridge, follow-up and food arrangements, not only phone numbers.
notes.body:
Denise lost employer insurance three months ago and now has variable income from two part-time jobs. She reports insufficient food during the past month and sometimes skips meals so her daughter can eat.

With her consent I began benefits screening and requested income documents for a manufacturer assistance application (simulated) and community health center enrollment. Medicaid and marketplace eligibility require formal review, and no coverage approval is documented today.

Her sister can continue childcare temporarily, while transportation and work-related scheduling remain barriers. We agreed that she will leave with an insulin and testing-supply bridge, a reachable follow-up team and specific food access arrangements rather than a list of telephone numbers alone.

notes.title: Nutrition Assessment - Affordable Carbohydrate Counting
notes.author: S. Lindholm, RD
notes.summary: Usual weight about 64 kg, ED weight 60 kg while dehydrated. Irregular meals from work schedules and grocery shortages. Plan: about 45 g carbohydrate per meal, practice with affordable foods; flexible carbohydrate-based insulin if fixed doses prove unsafe.
notes.body:
Denise's usual weight is approximately 64 kg and the ED weight was 60 kg during dehydration. She describes irregular meals driven by work schedules and grocery shortages rather than a preference for skipping food.

We practiced identifying affordable carbohydrate portions using beans, oats, rice, milk and shelf-stable foods. Today's plan uses approximately 45 g carbohydrate per meal while staff document what she actually eats.

She understands that meal insulin should match food, but says her appetite is still unpredictable after the vomiting illness. I will coordinate food resources and recommend a flexible carbohydrate-based insulin plan if fixed meal doses prove unsafe.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Event Note - Low Glucose After Lunch
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: Glucose 62 at 1400 with shakiness and sweating after lispro 4 units at 1145 and only 15 g of lunch eaten. 15 g juice: 78 at 1415, snack, 104 at 1430. Symptoms resolved. Meal insulin now by carbohydrate actually eaten (order 1435); glargine continues.
notes.body:
At 1400 Denise reported shakiness and sweating and the bedside glucose was 62. She had received the 1145 lispro dose for a planned 45 g lunch but ate only 15 g because her appetite declined.

She was awake with a safe swallow, so she received 120 mL of juice (15 g rapid carbohydrate). Glucose rose to 78 at 1415, a protein-containing 15 g carbohydrate snack followed, and the glucose was 104 at 1430. Symptoms have resolved. I was notified; the next stability check is due at 1500.

The 1435 order replaces fixed meal doses with insulin matched to the carbohydrate actually eaten, and basal insulin continues after review. Endocrinology is reviewing the doses.

notes.title: Endocrinology Dose Review - Hypoglycemia
notes.author: V. Lee, MD
notes.summary: The low followed a fixed meal dose with a small meal. Repeat values responded to oral treatment; no new ketoacidosis. Fixed 4-unit meal dose stopped at 1435; lispro 1 unit per 15 g eaten, given just after eating. Glargine 18 units continues.
notes.body:
Today's hypoglycemia followed a clear mismatch between a fixed nutritional insulin dose and the amount of lunch consumed. Repeat glucose values show response to oral treatment, and there is no recurrent vomiting or evidence of renewed ketoacidosis.

At 1435 I discontinued the fixed 4-unit meal order and prescribed lispro at one unit per 15 g carbohydrate actually eaten, given just after eating while appetite is uncertain (rounded down to a whole unit). Keep the conservative premeal correction and give no bedtime correction.

Continue glargine 18 units daily because fasting and overnight values do not suggest excess basal insulin. Nursing and the dietitian will rehearse carbohydrate estimation using meals she can afford and foods available during work shifts.

notes.title: Pharmacy Access and Affordability Review
notes.author: H. Price, PharmD
notes.summary: A manufacturer savings program for people without insurance (simulated, about $35 per month) would cover one long-acting and one rapid-acting pen when filled together. A hospital charity fund (simulated) will cover the first fill and supplies. Application still being assembled; nothing delivered yet.
notes.body:
The dispensing pharmacy has verified that a long-acting pen (glargine) and a rapid-acting pen (lispro) can be filled together under a manufacturer savings program for people without insurance (simulated, about $35 per month for the two insulins together). That figure does not cover meter strips, pen needles or other supplies.

Her lispro is one product only: the discharge reconciliation will replace her former fixed 6-unit instruction rather than add a second rapid-acting product. A simulated hospital charity fund will cover the first fill, pen needles, meter supplies, ketone strips, glucose treatment and glucagon while a patient-assistance application (simulated) is pursued.

The application is still being assembled and no approval or shipment has occurred. The community health center will own application follow-up and renewal checks, including reassessment if her insurance status changes. Delivery to the bedside is planned but has not occurred, so this note alone does not satisfy discharge readiness.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Night Note - Pen Teach-Back
notes.author: T. Rivera, MD
notes.summary: At the 2030 teach-back Denise first named the meal-insulin pen as the afternoon pen; similar-looking pens. Labeled demonstration pens and a one-page schedule used; correct on repeat, still needs written prompts for the missed-meal plan. Educator to repeat tomorrow. Dinner tolerated, 3 units after 45 g.
notes.body:
The night nurse reports that during the 2030 demonstration Denise initially identified the meal-insulin pen as the pen to use every afternoon. She said the similar-looking pens made it hard to remember which insulin must continue when she does not eat.

Using labeled demonstration pens and a one-page schedule, the nurse reviewed basal insulin at 1630 and lispro matched to carbohydrate. She correctly identified both pens on an immediate repeat attempt but still needed written prompts to explain the missed-meal plan.

Dinner was tolerated (45 g eaten, lispro 3 units at 1920, glucose 174 before the meal) and she has had no further hypoglycemia symptoms this evening. Another independent demonstration with the diabetes educator is requested tomorrow.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Night Note - Overnight Summary
notes.author: T. Rivera, MD
notes.summary: Rested overnight, no nausea or low-glucose symptoms; bedtime 162, 0200 check 140. Identifies the basal pen by its label. Worried about strips and time off work. 0645 labs not yet due.
notes.body:
Denise rested overnight without nausea, vomiting or symptoms of hypoglycemia. The bedtime glucose was 162 and the ordered 0200 safety check was 140.

She can identify the basal pen using the printed label and says the separate timing now makes more sense. She remains concerned about obtaining strips and finding time for follow-up between jobs.

The 0645 blood specimen is not yet due and no morning chemistry result is available. Handoff will emphasize independent pen identification, bedside supply verification and completion of the food and transportation plan.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Progress Note - Day 3 Morning
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: 0645 panel: K 4.1, bicarbonate 25, gap 9, creatinine 0.7, phosphate 2.9. Prebreakfast glucose 134, no overnight lows. Rehydrated, eating, walking. Continue basal and carbohydrate-matched meal insulin. Discharge depends on medicines in hand, follow-up and independent teach-back.
notes.body:
The 0645 panel is available with potassium 4.1, bicarbonate 25, anion gap 9, creatinine 0.7 and phosphate 2.9. Prebreakfast glucose is 134 with no recurrent low readings overnight.

She is clinically rehydrated, eating and ambulating independently. Continue the current basal and carbohydrate-matched meal insulin.

Discharge remains contingent on medicines and supplies in hand, reliable follow-up and independent teach-back after last night's pen confusion. Pharmacy delivery and case-management review are planned for today but are not yet complete.

notes.title: Pharmacy Bedside Delivery - Discharge Supplies
notes.author: H. Price, PharmD
notes.summary: Delivered at 1000: glargine and lispro pens (5 each), 200 pen needles, meter, 200 strips, 200 lancets, ketone strips, glucose tablets, glucagon kit. Labels match the plan (glargine 18 units at 1630; lispro 1 unit per 15 g). Former lispro instructions discontinued; no second product.
notes.body:
At 1000 the pharmacy delivered insulin glargine U-100 and insulin lispro U-100, each as a box of five 3 mL pens. The bag also contains 200 pen needles, a meter, 200 matching strips, 200 lancets, ketone strips, glucose tablets and a glucagon kit.

Labels specify glargine 18 units at 1630 and lispro one unit per 15 g carbohydrate with the written correction scale. Denise and I checked that her former fixed 6-unit lispro instructions are discontinued, that only one lispro product is listed and that no second basal product is listed.

The hospital charity fund (simulated) covered this discharge bridge. The working paid route for the next 30-day fill is the manufacturer savings program for people without insurance (simulated, about $35 per month for the two insulins together). We reviewed storage, expiration after opening, safe disposal and the need to contact the clinic before supplies fall below one week.

notes.title: Case Management Coordination - Follow-Up and Assistance
notes.author: A. Patel, RN CM
notes.summary: Riverbend Community Health Center (simulated) will see her Friday Nov 13 at 1000 (sliding fee $10, simulated); nurse call Nov 13 0830; diabetes education Nov 18 at 1500. Assistance application submitted, approval pending; clinic access coordinator checks Nov 16. Rides arranged.
notes.body:
Riverbend Community Health Center (simulated) has accepted Denise for a Friday, November 13 appointment at 1000 with a sliding-fee visit charge of $10 (simulated). A diabetes-education follow-up is booked for November 18 at 1500, and a clinic nurse telephone check is booked for November 13 at 0830.

The completed manufacturer-assistance application (simulated) has now been submitted with her income documents, but approval is still pending. The clinic's access coordinator has accepted responsibility for checking the application on November 16 and keeping a bridge available if processing is delayed.

A round-trip ride for the first appointment and a ride home tomorrow have been arranged. Denise has the clinic contact card and understands that she must report any price, refill, coverage or food problem before insulin runs out.

notes.title: Nutrition and Food-Resource Follow-Up
notes.author: S. Lindholm, RD
notes.summary: Correctly estimated today's 60 g lunch and its 4-unit lispro dose with supervision; practiced a 30 g meal (2 units). Community pantry food box reserved for her sister; school meal support and SNAP referral documented. No carbohydrate eaten = no meal lispro; basal continues.
notes.body:
Denise correctly estimated today's 60 g lunch and the corresponding 4-unit lispro dose with nursing supervision. We practiced an alternative 30 g meal that would need only 2 nutritional units under her current plan.

A community food pantry has reserved a food box for her sister to collect this afternoon, and school meal support and a SNAP application referral are documented. Denise chose shelf-stable items she can carry between jobs and agreed to keep a rapid carbohydrate source with her meter.

She understands that eating no carbohydrate means no nutritional lispro dose, while basal insulin continues and correction or illness questions follow the written plan. The clinic dietitian will review meal access and carbohydrate estimates at follow-up rather than assuming she can purchase a special diet.

notes.title: Diabetes Education - Final Assessment
notes.author: O. Hart, RN, CDCES
notes.summary: Identified both pens from the labels without prompting; demonstrated meter use, priming, dose selection, site rotation, sharps disposal. Gave glargine 18 units at 1630 under supervision. Taught back low-glucose treatment, illness rules and when to seek urgent care. Sister took part.
notes.body:
Denise independently identified glargine and lispro from their labels without prompting. She demonstrated meter use, pen priming, dose selection, injection-site rotation and safe needle disposal. At 1630 she administered the prescribed 18-unit glargine dose under RN supervision.

She calculated doses for 15 g, 30 g, 45 g and 60 g meals and explained how she would handle a missed meal. She correctly taught back low-glucose treatment, continued basal insulin during illness, ketone checks, and urgent evaluation for persistent vomiting or DKA symptoms.

Her sister participated with consent, and both can locate the written schedule, clinic contact card, food plan and medication bag.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Night Note - Discharge Readiness
notes.author: T. Rivera, MD
notes.summary: 1845 panel: K 4.1, bicarbonate 26, gap 9, phosphate 3.1; glucose 156 before dinner. Medicines and supplies are at the bedside; independent teach-back documented this afternoon. Sister will collect the food box and take her home. Final chemistry and the discharge decision are for the morning.
notes.body:
The 1845 panel has released with potassium 4.1, bicarbonate 26, anion gap 9 and phosphate 3.1. The pre-dinner glucose was 156 and her dinner tray has arrived.

She has correctly explained the expected meal dose, which will be given after the amount eaten is confirmed. Her labeled discharge medicines and supplies are at the bedside and the educator documented independent teach-back this afternoon. Her sister has confirmed collection of the food box and plans to bring her home tomorrow.

Final chemistry and the discharge decision remain scheduled for the morning and are not yet available.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Note - Conditional Discharge
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: Completed the evening self-management demonstration and tolerated dinner; bedtime glucose 144, no lows or DKA symptoms. Medicines, supplies, follow-up and transport verified. Conditional discharge order for 0700, pending the final chemistry (0645 specimen not yet resulted).
notes.body:
Denise completed the evening self-management demonstration under supervision and tolerated dinner. The bedtime glucose was 144, and no symptoms of recurrent hypoglycemia or DKA occurred overnight.

Her medicine and supply bridge, written regimen, follow-up appointments and transportation arrangements have been verified. I have written a conditional discharge order for 0700, contingent on the final chemistry and glucose review.

The 0645 specimen is pending, so this note does not attest to its results. If those results show recurrent acidosis or significant electrolyte abnormalities, cancel the discharge and reassess treatment.

notes.title: Case Management Final Verification
notes.author: A. Patel, RN CM
notes.summary: Sister confirmed the ride. Clinic visit and next-day call remain booked; contact card in hand. Food box collected; daughter supervised. Assistance application pending (clinic checks Nov 16). Denise understands the paid refill fallback and will call the clinic if cost, work, transport or food threatens the plan.
notes.body:
Denise's sister has confirmed that she will arrive for the planned discharge ride. The community health center appointment and next-day telephone check remain booked, and Denise has the printed contact card. The food box was collected yesterday and the daughter has safe supervision.

Manufacturer assistance remains pending (simulated), with the clinic access coordinator assigned to check progress on November 16. Denise has a supplied medication bridge and understands the working refill fallback instead of relying on an assumed assistance approval.

She agrees to call the clinic if a pharmacy charge, work schedule, transportation problem or food shortage threatens the plan.

notes.title: Hospital Medicine Discharge Note
notes.author: D. Reed, MD
notes.summary: Final chemistry: K 4.2, bicarbonate 26, gap 9, creatinine 0.7, phosphate 3.2, Mg 2.0; glucose 134. Discharge criteria met. Glargine 18 units next due today at 1630; breakfast lispro by carbohydrate eaten. Saline lock out, teach-back done with Denise and her sister. Leaves with her sister.
notes.body:
The final chemistry is now available with potassium 4.2, bicarbonate 26, anion gap 9, creatinine 0.7, phosphate 3.2 and magnesium 2.0. The prebreakfast bedside glucose is 134, and the conditional discharge criteria are met.

Denise correctly states that her next glargine dose is 18 units at 1630 today and that breakfast lispro depends on the carbohydrate she actually eats after leaving. She has the labeled medication bag, meter and supplies, low-glucose rescue treatment, written sick-day plan and follow-up contact card. No antibiotics, anticoagulant, IV fluid or electrolyte prescription is needed at discharge.

The remaining peripheral IV is removed intact and discharge instructions are reviewed with Denise and her sister using teach-back. She leaves with her sister without recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms or unresolved medication-access needs for the supplied bridge period.
